Daniel’s comparison is suggestive, but it rests on an unstated premise: that the “resemblance” is primarily a shared trick of self-reference, when the more interesting commonality is a shared stance toward *telos*—the suspicion that songs (and by extension arguments, days, and lives) need a “why” at all. Hofstadter’s Crab is literally praising a lyric that ends “without why or wherefore,” and Wurtz’s “before you know it, it’ll be Tuesday” lands with a similar anti-climax: not a punchline, not a moral, just the calendar reasserting itself. Read that way, the link is less “Bill Wurtz does Hofstadter” than “both works dramatize how easily our minds retrofit purpose onto sequences that may be mostly momentum.” That’s a recognizably Hofstadterian theme from *[Gödel, Escher, Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del,_Escher,_Bach)*—the mind’s compulsion to manufacture pattern and meaning—yet Daniel doesn’t quite name what is being patterned here: not just a self-referential wink, but a critique of narrative causality.

A second blind spot is that Daniel frames the kinship as textual (endings, lines, resemblance) while underplaying how *form* does the philosophical work. Wurtz’s piece is 40 seconds of rapid promise (“I’m gonna show you…”) collapsing into ordinary time; the joke depends on tempo, tonal sincerity, and the contrast between self-help grandiosity and a weekday. Hofstadter’s verse, by contrast, is a stylized, almost courtly meta-compliment. If the point is that both enact “meaning without reason,” then it matters that Wurtz achieves it through pop compression and whiplash, while Hofstadter achieves it through a literary frame that explicitly invites the reader to notice the trick. Without that distinction, “resemblance” risks becoming a synonym for “they both break expectations,” which is true but thin.

Finally, the blog’s “closing remark referencing itself” is a nice nod to Hofstadter, but it also exposes a question Daniel doesn’t ask: when does self-reference add insight, and when is it merely decorative cleverness? Traditions like *[metafiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metafiction)* and constraint-based play (e.g., *[Oulipo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oulipo)*) show both possibilities. A stronger ending would briefly state what the self-reference *buys* the reader here—e.g., that the post itself enacts the same move it points to: it refuses to conclude with a thesis, and instead lets “Tuesday” (the arbitrary endpoint) stand in for closure. If that’s Daniel’s intent, making it explicit would turn a private salute into a public argument.
